notes.meaning: The sufferer calls out to the Lord with urgent cries for help. He brings his pain honestly before God because he has nowhere else to turn. Even when feeling faint and overwhelmed, believers can pour out their laments to God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted this opening prayer as the voice of Christ crying out to the Father during His passion.

notes.meaning: The psalmist begs God not to turn away in his dark hour, but to lean down and answer him right away. Trouble feels unbearable when it seems like God is far off or hiding His face. Sufferers long for a quick word of comfort from the Lord.

The writer feels his life slipping away like smoke disappearing in the air. His bones feel scorched, as if burning on a blazing hearth. Extreme physical pain and inner distress have drained all his strength.

His heart feels like grass cut down and dried out under the hot sun. He is so weighed down with grief that he even forgets to eat his daily meals. Deep emotional sorrow often robs the body of its normal appetite.
Constant groaning and lack of food have worn his body down to skin and bones. His intense pain has caused severe physical wasting. Sorrow in the soul quickly shows itself in the weakness of the body.

The psalmist compares himself to lonely birds, like an owl dwelling among desolate desert ruins. These birds were known for their sad cries and solitary living far from people. He feels totally deserted and cut off from the comfort of others.

Sleepless nights add to his misery as he lies awake watching through the dark hours. He feels like a lone bird sitting perched on a rooftop, apart from the flock. Loneliness is especially painful when rest will not come.

His enemies mock and insult him all day long without stopping. They even use his name and tragic situation as a curse against others, wishing his misery upon their own foes. Being ridiculed by enemies makes deep affliction cut even harder.

Sitting in dust and mourning has made ashes as common to him as daily bread. Tears stream down his face, mixing into whatever he tries to drink. His whole life is steeped in bitter sorrow and deep humiliation.

Worst of all is the feeling that God's own anger is directed against him. He feels as though God picked him up like a whirlwind only to throw him violently to the ground. The heaviest burden in any trial is the fear that the Lord is displeased.

His days are like the long evening shadows that quickly fade into the black of night. He feels himself withering away like cut grass nearing the end of its life. Looking at human life alone reminds us of how frail and short our time on earth is.

The psalmist abruptly turns his eyes from his own weakness to God's eternal throne. Human beings quickly fade away, but the Lord reigns forever and His name will never be forgotten. Remembering God's unchanging nature brings steady hope when our personal strength fails.

The writer expresses confidence that the Lord will soon rise up and show mercy to Jerusalem. He believes the set time of seventy years prophesied for exile is finally being fulfilled. God never forgets His timetable for restoring His people.

God's faithful servants still cherish the ruined stones and dust of Jerusalem. Even when the holy city lies in rubble, it remains precious in the eyes of those who love God's house. True devotion loves God's people and His work even in seasons of ruin and defeat.

When the Lord restores His city, neighboring nations and their kings will look on with reverent awe. God's marvelous deliverance of His people reveals His majesty to the wider world. The restoration of God's church serves as a witness to the whole earth.

The rebuilding of Zion will display the Lord's glorious presence and power. Rebuilding what was completely destroyed is something only God could accomplish. When the Lord renews His church, He makes His saving glory clear to all.

The Lord will not overlook the cries of His ruined, helpless people. Even though the exiles were stripped bare of earthly power and standing, God listens carefully to their pleas. God never despises the prayer of someone who has nothing left to offer.

This mighty act of mercy must be written down so future generations will know it. People who are not yet born will read the record and praise the Lord for His faithfulness. God preserves the story of His grace in Scripture so that every new generation can trust Him.

The Lord bends down His gaze from His high, heavenly sanctuary to look upon the earth. Though He is exalted above all creation, He pays close attention to the troubles of mortal men. God's high throne never removes Him from knowing our earthly struggles.

God looks down specifically to hear the groans of captives suffering in chains. He steps in to free prisoners who were sentenced to die in exile. The Lord specializes in rescuing people who have no hope of saving themselves.

The ransomed prisoners are set free so they can publicly tell what God has done. They will fill Jerusalem and Zion with songs of thanksgiving and testimony to His name. Deliverance from trouble gives believers a new song to share among God's people.

This praise will expand until nations and kingdoms unite together to worship the Lord. Both Jews and Gentiles will gather in one great assembly to offer Him service. God's plan of redemption has always looked toward gathering the whole world to Himself.

The psalmist turns back to his own fragile life, confessing that God has sapped his strength along the journey. His days have been cut short in the middle of life's course. Sickness and affliction remind us that our physical vitality is completely in God's hands.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine, following the Greek Septuagint wording, understood this verse as the unified Church answering God about her days.

notes.meaning: The writer pleads with God not to let him die halfway through his life. He contrasts his own short lifespan with God's years, which continue through all generations without end. When we face our own mortality, our only refuge is God's eternal life.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted this as the Church praying to survive until the end of the world, refuting opponents who claimed she had died out.

notes.meaning: Long ago, God laid the foundations of the solid earth, and His hands shaped the heavens. The universe did not make itself, but was brought into being by God's creative wisdom. Creation itself stands as living proof of the Lord's power.

Even the sky and earth, which seem so stable to humans, will eventually wear out like an old cloak. God will change them and fold them up just like a person changes clothes. Nothing in all creation lasts forever except the Creator Himself.

While all created things decay, the Lord remains exactly the same, and His years will never end. The New Testament applies these very words to Jesus Christ, showing His eternal divine nature. We can place our trust in a Savior who never changes and never dies.

Because the Lord lives forever, the children of His servants will dwell safely in His presence. Their descendants will stand firm and secure before Him across the coming generations. Believers rest in the comfort that God's covenant promises extend to their children after them.
